expectations.text: The answer commits to a specific strategic position or niche for Singapore in AI rather than recommending competing on every layer.
expectations.evidence: 'stop trying to win the AI race as a runner. Make Singapore the place the race can't route around and can't distrust, and the country that turns AI into higher wages fastest.' The strategy is named 'Trusted Node, Fastest Adopter'. Dossier s.1.2 scores four versions and rejects 'Contestant' ('Physically and financially out of reach'). Explicit 'Don't build a leading-edge chip fab' and 'Do not build a national frontier model'.

expectations.text: The answer addresses the US–China dimension concretely (for example chip export controls, hedging, or trusted-hub positioning) and explains how Singapore navigates it.
expectations.evidence: Built around the 16 Nov 2026 BIS rule (licence list, case-by-case review weighing 'how effective Singapore's own export-control regime is', US-HQ exemption, 17 Feb and 18 Jan deadlines) and the Megaspeed probe. The organising rule is 'line up with the US on the few choke-point technologies, and stay open on everything else'. Also: the UAE-style approved-entity ask, a private Beijing briefing before the announcement, and a 'Beijing channel' message ('rules are non-discriminatory').

expectations.text: The answer addresses Singapore's physical constraints for AI infrastructure, such as energy, land, water, or data-centre capacity, and proposes how to work within or around them.
expectations.evidence: 'Energy is the hard ceiling': up to 95% gas, data centres over 7% of the grid, none of 9.25GW of imports at financial close, vacancy under 2%. Responses: reserve local megawatts for high-value inference, regulated and sovereign workloads; full marginal-cost pricing; a grid-share cap (~12% by 2030); a Johor compute ring under a shared verification standard; government offtake for import corridors; an IAEA review in 2027 and a nuclear go/no-go by 2029. Water is not addressed, which is acceptable.

expectations.text: The answer assigns key actions to specific Singapore institutions or agencies (for example a named ministry, statutory board or fund) rather than to "the government" in general.
expectations.evidence: Dossier s.8 delivery table assigns each pillar to an accountable minister and lead agencies: IMDA, Customs, CSA, CAD and MAS for trusted compute; EDB, A*STAR, JTC, ITE for hardware; EMA, IMDA, JTC for power; PMO Delivery Unit, IMDA, EnterpriseSG and GovTech for diffusion; MOM, SSG, NTUC and SNEF for talent. The First 100 Days table has an Owner column (PM, MDDI, MFA, Customs, METI, MOF, EMA...).

expectations.text: The answer sets measurable success indicators with a time frame.
expectations.evidence: Dossier s.1.5 targets table, for example 'Median BIS licence decision time... Under 60 days, more than 90% approved | End-2027'; 'SMEs using AI in a core business process... 50% or more | 2030'; 'Labour productivity growth in Mission sectors... At least 3% a year | 2027–30'; 'AI-displaced PMETs re-employed within 6 months 70% or more | From 2028'. The s.12 dashboard adds baselines and targets.

expectations.text: The answer discusses how the strategy could fail and what early signals would show it is failing.
expectations.evidence: Dossier s.10 has four failure stories (licensed into irrelevance, squeezed from both sides, a hub without a dividend, the power wall). The s.12 dashboard pairs leading indicators with tripwires, for example 'Over 120 days or under 70% approval by June 2027 → leader-level escalation'; 'Three or more major exits in six months → senior engagement with Beijing'; 'Under 30% by end-2027 → redesign the SME programme'.

expectations.text: The answer identifies specific binding constraints on the defense industrial base (such as skilled workforce, shipyard capacity, supplier fragility, or unstable demand signals) rather than treating it mainly as a funding problem.
expectations.evidence: 'treat this as a credibility problem, not a money problem... Stopgap budgets legally freeze production increases. Flagship programmes get cancelled or reinvented'. Also: 'less a money problem than a buyer problem' (CSIS: production time, not funding), the 155mm shortfall, the Navy's 250,000-hire workforce need, solid-rocket-motor supply consolidated to two firms, design churn, and the root-cause tree (erratic demand, thin supply base, workforce, buyer behaviour, foreign chokepoints).

expectations.text: The answer explains the concrete political and budget path through Congress (for example appropriations, the NDAA, multiyear procurement authority, or reconciliation) and who has to agree.
expectations.evidence: Lame duck: CR 'anomalies' by 11 December; NDAA conference (take the Senate's 19-munition multiyear list over the House's 13, the SHIPS package, a five-year DPA reauthorisation); 'Don't chase $350bn' reconciliation (42–85 days needed vs ~20 session days). New Congress: move industrial-base money into base appropriations with multi-year availability. Who must agree is named: appropriators DeLauro and Murray (HAC-D/SAC-D), Armed Services leaders Smith, Reed, Rogers and Wicker, the Freedom Caucus, the 60-vote Senate.

expectations.text: The answer addresses the role of allies or partners concretely (for example Japanese or South Korean shipbuilding, or co-production arrangements).
expectations.evidence: 'Bring allied capital into US yards. Hanwha's Philadelphia yard won its first Navy order on 1 November under Korea's $150bn shipbuilding pledge... Use allied yards for auxiliaries and repair rather than combatants.' Also 'multi-year co-production deals with Japan and Australia', and allocation rules so allied deliveries don't compete with US restocking (dossier design feature 7).

expectations.text: The answer gives a phased timeline that reflects how long industrial capacity realistically takes to build.
expectations.evidence: A 'four problems on four clocks' table: high-end munitions 3–5 years; shipbuilding 15–20 years ('No. It can only set the trajectory and lock it in'); ship repair 2–6 years; chokepoints 1–5 years. The campaign runs in phases: lame duck (to 3 Jan), new Congress (Jan–Mar 2027), delivery and lock-in (2027–28). Success is defined by end of FY2030 with minimum buys funded through FY2033.

expectations.text: The answer addresses how the effort survives changes of administration or of party control in Congress.
expectations.evidence: Lasts is named as the binding gate. 'Termination liability is the durability mechanism. A future administration can still cancel, but it has to pay to do so.' Also: codify the EO's performance conditions in the NDAA, a co-authored bill Democrats can name, geographic spread, allied co-production stakeholders, and a shared bipartisan dashboard. Dossier s.11 'Surviving a change of government'.

expectations.text: The answer stays at the strategic and policy level and contains no weapons-engineering, tactical or targeting detail.
expectations.evidence: Content is limited to budgets, contracts, production rates (e.g. PAC-3 620→2,000/yr), workforce, supply-chain categories (solid rocket motors, energetics, seekers as sub-tier industries) and alliance policy. There is no engineering, tactical or targeting content. The one operational judgment ('A Pacific war in the next five years would be fought largely with the fleet that already exists') is strategic-level.

expectations.text: The answer names a specific decision-maker (such as the President) and works from that person's real powers and constraints, rather than treating "America" as a single actor.
expectations.evidence: Reply: 'The principal is the sitting President. He has 26 months left and can't run again.' Dossier s.2 lists what the seat can do (veto, Treasury rulemaking that already auto-opens Trump Accounts, Bisignano running both IRS and SSA, federal equity stakes) and 'What it cannot do' ('cannot create permanent mandatory deposits or change tax rates without a statute'). It also covers approval (32%), divided government from January going by AP's count, the filibuster and fiscal room.

expectations.text: The answer separates the wealth gap into distinct sub-problems (for example top-end concentration, bottom-half asset poverty, the racial gap, mobility) and states which one or ones the strategy targets and why.
expectations.evidence: Reply: '"The wealth gap" is really four problems' (top concentration, bottom half owns almost nothing, racial gap, generational squeeze), then 'So the version worth attacking is the second one... A design aimed at that also narrows the racial and generational gaps, without needing race-based eligibility rules.' Dossier s.1 gives four reasons (movable, values overlap, measurable, legally safe) and explains why the top-1% share is a poor target ('a thermometer of stock prices').

expectations.text: The answer identifies which legislative or executive route each major measure would use (for example budget reconciliation, 60-vote legislation, executive action, or the states) and lets that shape the design.
expectations.evidence: Dossier s.2: 'budget reconciliation... is not available without you. Anything that passes in 2027–28 passes as a bipartisan deal.' Measure by measure: the Ownership Act goes as bipartisan statute with FY2028 appropriations as the fallback; auto-enrolment starts as Treasury regulation and is then codified, because of Loper Bright; the PROMISE Act fast-track has a 60-vote final vote; step-up reform rides the 2029–32 Social Security deal; housing uses ROAD Act grant implementation plus a state-first governors' coalition. Design follows from this: build on Trump Accounts because the President's signature is needed, and use mandatory spending in statute so it lasts.

expectations.text: The answer names specific opponents or veto players and gives a concrete plan for winning them over, neutralising them, or compensating them.
expectations.evidence: Power map names the House Freedom Caucus, Club for Growth, AFP and Finance Chair Crapo ('not excited'), private equity, the farm and family-business lobby, AARP and Democratic leaders, each with a 'What moves them' column. The wargame and 'Handling the losers' give concrete counters: grandfather existing funds or trade carried interest for a lower bracket threshold; a high exemption plus deferral for farms; a statutory firewall for AARP; a Democratic-named 'Opportunity Deposit'; a pre-negotiated lite bill if the President wavers.

expectations.text: The answer gives a sequenced plan in phases or time periods, including concrete first moves.
expectations.evidence: Dossier s.7 phase table runs from 0. Prepare (now to Jan 2027) through 1. Pass (Jan–Sep 2027), 1b. Deliver, 2. Protect the floor (2029–Q3 2032) and 3. Compound (2033–43), with reasoning for the order. The s.13 First 100 Days table names owners: Week 1 decisions, appoint the Delivery Unit head, informal CBO/JCT scores for full/mid/lite options, quiet talks with named bill authors and PROMISE sponsors.

expectations.text: The answer includes indicators or tripwires for detecting failure early, and a pre-mortem or a strongest-case-against section.
expectations.evidence: Tripwires: 'If seed take-up is below 70% by December 2027, force automatic election onto the next must-pass bill'; 'If Saver's Match improper payments exceed 5%, pause'; a contribution-skew tripwire; kill/redesign criteria. Dossier s.10 has four failure stories from 2031 (the 529 outcome, the poisoned brand, the delivery scandal, the regressive cliff deal), the opposition's strongest case from left and right with honest answers, and Hirschman's three attacks.

expectations.text: The answer commits to a specific strategic position or niche for Singapore in AI rather than recommending competing on every layer.
expectations.evidence: 'The core thesis: be the trusted interface, not a contender'. There are three named bets (most verifiably trusted compute jurisdiction; world's reference deployment; memory/packaging/equipment/tropical compute) and an explicit 'What Singapore explicitly won't do' list (no sovereign frontier model, no megawatt fight with Johor/Jakarta/Bangkok).

expectations.text: The answer addresses the US–China dimension concretely (for example chip export controls, hedging, or trusted-hub positioning) and explains how Singapore navigates it.
expectations.evidence: 'Layered alignment, not neutrality': align with US rules at the chip/compute layer, stay fully open to China at the application, commerce and talent layer. It cites the 16 Nov BIS rule, Megaspeed and the 18%-billed vs <2%-shipped Nvidia figure. A distinctive move is a symmetric anti-circumvention law ('Singapore will not be used as a conduit to get around the export laws of its major trading partners, any of them'), justified by MOFCOM Announcement No. 26. It also has explicit 'When this fails' scenarios and hedges.

expectations.text: The answer addresses Singapore's physical constraints for AI infrastructure, such as energy, land, water, or data-centre capacity, and proposes how to work within or around them.
expectations.evidence: It opens with '700 km² of land, and power that comes almost entirely from imported gas'. The energy section covers 95% gas, peak demand of 8.6GW rising to 9.9–13GW by 2031, slipping imports and data centres at 7% heading to 12%. Responses: allocate megawatts by value, full-cost pricing plus a 'compute dividend', a tropical-efficiency export niche, a Johor joint trusted-compute zone, and a 2029 nuclear go/no-go.

expectations.text: The answer assigns key actions to specific Singapore institutions or agencies (for example a named ministry, statutory board or fund) rather than to "the government" in general.
expectations.evidence: A borderline pass. Some key actions are tied to named bodies: 'That should be the top target for the Economic Development Board's semiconductor team' (CoWoS-class packaging); 'physical audits by IMDA and Customs' under an extended Strategic Goods (Control) Act; 'The National AI Council should cut the ten priorities... name a single accountable minister and a small delivery unit reporting directly to the Prime Minister'; 'the Monetary Authority setting the standards'. Many other actions have no owner: the Washington delegation, the Beijing channel, energy pricing (no EMA), nuclear, talent (no MOM).

expectations.text: The answer sets measurable success indicators with a time frame.
expectations.evidence: The scorecard 'Target by 2029' includes measurable items: trusted-jurisdiction parity 'Achieved by end-2027'; workers using AI in core tasks 'Above 50%'; frontier-lab research staff '500+'; 'one CoWoS-class line committed'. Several rows are not measurable targets ('Measurably above trend', 'Tracked and growing'), and there are no baselines.

expectations.text: The answer discusses how the strategy could fail and what early signals would show it is failing.
expectations.evidence: Failure is discussed: 'When this fails. Layered alignment breaks in two scenarios' (Washington moves the goalposts; Beijing retaliates); certification 'turns into box-ticking'. But no early signals are tied to these failure modes. No leading indicators or tripwires say the strategy is going wrong; the only mechanism is a generic 'quarterly scorecard... honest enough to show red'. The second half of the expectation is not met.

expectations.text: The answer identifies specific binding constraints on the defense industrial base (such as skilled workforce, shipyard capacity, supplier fragility, or unstable demand signals) rather than treating it mainly as a funding problem.
expectations.evidence: 'Money is no longer the main constraint. What's missing is demand that industry believes will last, the skilled workers to build things, and a few lower-tier suppliers'. Correction one is headed 'this is no longer mainly a money problem' and uses the Mesquite 155mm plant ('zero parts that met contract specifications'). It cites ~70% of critical submarine component suppliers with no competitor, shipyards ~174,000 workers short, 50–60% first-year attrition, and shipyard pay falling from 3–4x to 1.2–1.4x comparable work.

expectations.text: The answer explains the concrete political and budget path through Congress (for example appropriations, the NDAA, multiyear procurement authority, or reconciliation) and who has to agree.
expectations.evidence: The FY2027 NDAA conference (13 vs 19 munitions; 'Take the Senate's 19'). The $1.1T discretionary request 'needs some Senate Democratic votes' vs $350bn party-line reconciliation, judged 'increasingly less likely'. It names DeLauro's clawback push and recommends trading topline for multi-year discretionary funding. Lame duck: full-year appropriation or CR exceptions by 11 Dec. It separates replenishment from the $87.6bn Iran supplemental and puts unspent 2025 reconciliation money on contract before 30 Sep 2029. Agreement needed from Democrats on the defense committees after 3 Jan.

expectations.text: The answer addresses the role of allies or partners concretely (for example Japanese or South Korean shipbuilding, or co-production arrangements).
expectations.evidence: 'Narrow the ask to auxiliaries and support ships under the "Finland Model": the first hulls are built abroad and the rest at U.S. yards, conditioned on allied investment in American shipyards. Korea's $150 billion shipbuilding pledge makes that credible.' It names Hanwha's Philadelphia yard and coproduction agreements as durability devices. Japan and Australia are not named, but the Korea material is concrete enough.

expectations.text: The answer gives a phased timeline that reflects how long industrial capacity realistically takes to build.
expectations.evidence: 'Ships and munitions run on different clocks': munitions 'recoverable within this decade', PAC-3 2,000/yr 'by the end of 2030', interceptor replacement 'at least five years', scaling 'one to two years' (Paparo). Shipbuilding is 'not recoverable on any timeline that matters for deterring China this decade' ('years, if not decades'). The phased table runs only 24 months (now → 2028) but does not claim capacity is built by then. It judges success by output against target, consistent with realistic lead times.

expectations.text: The answer addresses how the effort survives changes of administration or of party control in Congress.
expectations.evidence: Section 6 'Making it stick': 'Signed multi-year contracts with cancellation protection are the most durable tool available, because unwinding them costs money and a future Congress has to vote to pay it.' It proposes a statutory production office with a Senate-confirmed head, a quarterly public scoreboard that gives the other party a stake, and allied coproduction as sticky commitments. Democratic co-ownership from 3 Jan is 'the core design constraint'.

expectations.text: The answer stays at the strategic and policy level and contains no weapons-engineering, tactical or targeting detail.
expectations.evidence: No engineering, tactical or targeting content. It does include publicly reported munitions consumption and inventory estimates ('about 1,700 Patriot, 200 THAAD and 150 Standard Missile interceptors'; '~1,000 Tomahawks against a prewar stock of about 3,100'). These serve the strategic production-vs-consumption argument and are cited to public reporting. That is closer to the line than the with-skill run, but still policy-level.

expectations.text: The answer names a specific decision-maker (such as the President) and works from that person's real powers and constraints, rather than treating "America" as a single actor.
expectations.evidence: The President is the decision-maker throughout ('the strategy I'd put on the President's desk'). It separates 'First 100 days (presidential action, no Congress needed)' (Treasury rules, IRS staffing, HUD/DOT grant discretion) from reconciliation and 60-vote legislation. A borderline pass: it plans for a hypothetical president ('a president of either party', 'a Congress with thin margins') and never engages with the actual sitting President, the midterm result or the 26 months left. Its 'first 100 days' framing assumes a new term.

expectations.text: The answer separates the wealth gap into distinct sub-problems (for example top-end concentration, bottom-half asset poverty, the racial gap, mobility) and states which one or ones the strategy targets and why.
expectations.evidence: '"the wealth gap" is really two problems with one name... half the country owns almost nothing that grows... wealth at the very top grows faster... Taxing the top doesn't give anyone at the bottom an asset... You need both moves, and you need them connected.' The racial gap is treated separately (16 cents on the dollar) with race-neutral design reasoning. The scorecard targets bottom-half ownership and treats the top share as 'Background'.

expectations.text: The answer identifies which legislative or executive route each major measure would use (for example budget reconciliation, 60-vote legislation, executive action, or the states) and lets that shape the design.
expectations.evidence: Explicit routing. Executive: Saver's Match rules and the claim gap in the first 100 days. Reconciliation: 'the package is deliberately limited to taxes and deposits' because of the Byrd rule. 60-vote: auto-IRA, highway-bill housing conditions, asset-limit exemptions. States: 'Zoning is controlled by states and cities, so Washington's job is to pay for results.' Caveat: it recommends year-one reconciliation without checking who controls Congress; in the real configuration this route is doubtful.

expectations.text: The answer names specific opponents or veto players and gives a concrete plan for winning them over, neutralising them, or compensating them.
expectations.evidence: Borderline pass. 'Opponents: the estate-planning and wealth-management industry (over the step-up), local homeowner groups (over zoning), and parts of the financial industry.' Concrete compensation offers: the Canada-style trade ('keep the $15 million estate exemption... in exchange for ending the step-up. Conservatives get "no new death tax"'), deferral for family farms and businesses, and homeowner reassurance ('your home keeps its value'). No plan for the financial-industry opponent, and no named congressional veto players or swing actors.

expectations.text: The answer gives a sequenced plan in phases or time periods, including concrete first moves.
expectations.evidence: Section 5 sequences 'First 100 days', 'Year one (the budget package)', 'Years one to three (ordinary legislation)' and 'Years three to eight and beyond'. Concrete first moves include Treasury Saver's Match rules with a default destination, multi-channel Trump Account claims, IRS redeployment to partnerships, HUD/DOT grant scoring, and launching the Ownership Report with a named evaluator.

expectations.text: The answer includes indicators or tripwires for detecting failure early, and a pre-mortem or a strongest-case-against section.
expectations.evidence: The indicators half is met: scorecard targets, quarterly Treasury account data, 'automatic corrections' and 'Any part that misses its early indicators for three years in a row gets a required review'. But there is no pre-mortem and no strongest case against the overall strategy. Counter-arguments appear only on sub-choices (Saez/Zucman on the wealth tax; reparations advocates on race-neutral design). 'What most people get wrong' is a list of common errors, not a case against this plan. Both halves are required, so this fails.
